tagline: Name the concept, then apply it to a person who is actually in the room.
description: The 2024 AP Psychology framework reorganised the course into five units aligned with the APA Introductory Psychology Initiative — biological bases, cognition, development and learning, social psychology and personality, and mental and physical health — with each unit weighted equally. Research methods and data interpretation moved out of a unit and into the science practices that are tested throughout, and the two free-response questions are now the Article Analysis Question and the Evidence-Based Question. This course is built around that structure: apply concepts to scenarios, read studies critically, and argue from evidence.

frqs.label: Q1
frqs.title: Article Analysis Question (AAQ)
frqs.prompt: You are given one summarised, peer-reviewed psychology study. Respond to the parts: (A) identify the type of research design and explain how you know; (B) identify the independent and dependent variables, or explain why the study has neither; (C) identify a statistic reported in the study and explain what it means, or calculate and interpret a measure of central tendency, variation or percentile rank from the data; (D) identify an ethical consideration the researchers addressed or failed to address; (E) identify one limitation of the study and explain how it restricts what can be concluded; (F) explain how a named psychological concept relates to the study's findings or to their real-world application.
rubric: Name the design precisely — experiment, correlational study, naturalistic observation, case study or meta-analysis — and point at the feature that decides it: manipulation plus random assignment means experimental.
Operationalise both variables. A dependent variable that is not measurable, or an independent variable with no levels, loses the point.

Read the number the study reports rather than the number you expected. A negative correlation is a relationship, not the absence of one; effect size is strength, statistical significance is unlikeliness under chance.
Ethics: informed consent or assent, protection from harm, confidentiality, permitted deception plus debriefing, and institutional review. Say which one the scenario shows.
Limitations must be a limitation, not a complaint. Sample size, sampling method, self-report bias, directionality and third variables, and confounds all count; 'it was in a lab' alone does not.
Part F is a concept-application point: define the concept and tie it explicitly to the study, not to psychology in general.

frqs.label: Q2
frqs.title: Evidence-Based Question (EBQ)
frqs.prompt: You are given three short research studies on a shared topic and a prompt asking you to take a position. Write an argument that (A) makes a defensible claim responding to the prompt, (B) supports it with specific evidence from at least two of the sources, and (C) uses at least one psychological concept accurately, defining it and connecting it to your reasoning.
rubric: The claim is a sentence that takes a side. 'Research is mixed' is a summary, not a claim.
Use two different sources and cite what each actually found — the finding, not just the study name.
Acknowledge the source that complicates your claim and explain why it does not defeat it. That is where the argument earns its keep.
The psychological concept must be defined correctly and applied to the evidence, not dropped in as decoration.
Write in prose. The reader is not awarding points for headings, bullets or restating the prompt.

units.title: Biological Bases of Behavior
units.summary: Heredity and environment, the nervous system, neurons, the brain, sleep and sensation — the machinery that makes behaviour possible.

topics.title: Interaction of Heredity and Environment
topics.summary: Behaviour genetics asks not whether genes or environment matter, but how they interact — and how the design of a study decides what it can claim.
keyIdeas: Heredity supplies a range of possible outcomes; environment determines where inside that range a trait lands.
Behaviour genetics uses twin, adoption and family studies to estimate how much variation in a trait is attributable to genetic variation.
Identical (monozygotic) twins share essentially all their DNA; fraternal (dizygotic) twins share about half, which is what makes the comparison informative.
Twin studies confound genes with shared environment unless the design separates them — twins raised apart do that.
Heritability describes a population's variation, never one individual's trait, and it changes when the environment changes.
Epigenetics: experience can change how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence.

lesson.title: Heredity, environment, and what a twin study can actually prove
objectives: Explain how behaviour genetics separates genetic from environmental influence.
Read a twin or adoption design and state exactly what it can and cannot conclude.
Distinguish heritability of a trait in a population from the causes of that trait in a person.
Give an example of gene–environment interaction and of epigenetic change.

body.text: Every AP Psychology question about nature and nurture is secretly a question about **research design**. If you can name the design and what it controls for, you can answer it; if you argue from intuition about which side 'wins', you will lose the point.
The comparison that does the work

Identical twins come from one fertilised egg and share effectively all of their DNA. Fraternal twins come from two eggs and share about half, like any pair of siblings. Both kinds of twin usually share a household, an income, a school and a pair of parents. So if identical twins resemble each other on a trait more than fraternal twins do, that extra resemblance has somewhere to come from: the extra DNA.

body.label: The confound
body.text: Twins raised together share genes **and** environment. A high identical-twin correlation is consistent with genetics, but it is also consistent with a shared environment that happens to affect identical twins more — parents and strangers treat identical twins more alike than fraternal twins. Adoption and twins-raised-apart designs are what break that tie, because they hold the environment roughly constant while varying relatedness, or the reverse.
Heritability is not what people think it means
Heritability is the proportion of the **variation** in a trait, **in a population**, that is associated with genetic variation. It is not a statement about an individual, and it is not fixed.

body.label: Worked example
body.text: Imagine every child in a country receives the same excellent nutrition. Height is still highly heritable — the remaining differences are largely genetic. Now imagine nutrition becomes wildly unequal. Heritability of height **falls**, because the environment is now doing more of the explaining. Nothing changed in anyone's DNA.
Interaction, not addition

items: **Gene–environment interaction**: the same environment produces different outcomes depending on genotype, and the same genotype produces different outcomes depending on environment. A genetic susceptibility to depression may never appear without a triggering stressor.
**Gene–environment correlation**: people select and shape environments that match their dispositions — a sociable child seeks out groups, which builds further sociability.
**Epigenetics**: chemical marks on DNA change whether a gene is read, and some of those marks respond to experience. The sequence is unchanged; the expression is not.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: 'Heritability of 0.6 for intelligence means 60% of my intelligence is genetic.' It does not. It means 60% of the differences between people in that population, at that time, are associated with genetic differences. Say 'variation in the population' and you keep the point.

Where this shows up on the exam: a short paragraph describing a study, then 'which conclusion is best supported?' The distractors are almost always claims the design cannot carry — causation from a correlational design, individual-level claims from a population statistic, or an environment conclusion from a design that held the environment constant.

vocabulary.definition: The study of how genetic and environmental variation produce variation in behaviour and traits.
Twins from a single fertilised egg; genetically identical.
Twins from two separate eggs; genetically like ordinary siblings.
The proportion of variation in a trait within a population associated with genetic variation.
Changes in gene expression caused by chemical modification of DNA or its packaging, without a change in sequence.
When the effect of the environment on a trait depends on genotype, or vice versa.

mistakes: Treating heritability as a property of an individual rather than of variation across a population.
Reading 'genes and environment interact' as 'genes and environment each contribute a share' — interaction means the effect of one depends on the other.
Assuming identical twins prove a genetic cause without considering that identical twins are treated more alike.
Ignoring that heritability estimates shift when environments become more or less uniform.
review: Why does comparing identical with fraternal twins isolate genetic influence?
What is the heritability of a trait in a population where everyone has the same environment?
Give one example each of gene–environment interaction and epigenetic change.

questions.prompt: A researcher reports that identical twins raised apart correlate more highly on shyness than fraternal twins raised together. Which conclusion does this design best support?
choices: Shyness is caused entirely by genes and cannot be changed by experience.
Genetic variation is associated with variation in shyness, because resemblance persists without a shared home.
Being raised apart causes children to become shyer.
Shyness in one individual is 60% genetic.
questions.explanation: Twins raised apart remove the shared-environment explanation, so the remaining resemblance points to genetic variation. The design still cannot support a claim about a single person's trait (choice D), a cause 'entirely' from genes (A), or an effect of being raised apart (C).

questions.prompt: Two countries have equally heritable height, but in one the heritability estimate is far higher. Which difference between the countries best explains it?
choices: One country has taller parents on average.
One country's children receive much more uniform nutrition than the other's.
One country measures height more accurately.
One country has more identical twins.
questions.explanation: Heritability is the share of variation attributable to genetic variation. When the environment becomes more uniform, environmental variation shrinks, so the genetic share of what remains grows — with no change in anyone's DNA.

topics.title: Overview of the Nervous System
topics.summary: The central and peripheral systems, their subdivisions, and the glia and plasticity that support them.
keyIdeas: Central nervous system = brain and spinal cord; peripheral nervous system = everything else.
The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle; the autonomic system controls glands and internal organs.
Sympathetic arousal prepares the body for action; parasympathetic activity restores and conserves.
Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information in; motor (efferent) neurons carry commands out; interneurons connect them.
Glial cells support, insulate and nourish neurons; myelin speeds conduction.
Neuroplasticity is the nervous system's capacity to reorganise after experience or injury, greatest early in life.

questions.prompt: After narrowly avoiding a collision, a driver's heart is pounding; ten minutes later it slows and digestion resumes. Which pair of systems produced this sequence?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic division mobilises for action; the parasympathetic division then calms and restores. Both are branches of the autonomic nervous system, which is itself part of the peripheral nervous system.

topics.title: The Neuron and Neural Firing
topics.summary: How a single neuron converts chemistry into electricity and back, and how drugs change the message.
keyIdeas: Dendrites receive, the soma integrates, the axon carries, terminal buttons release neurotransmitter.
Resting potential is negative inside; depolarisation opens the way to an action potential.
Action potentials are all-or-none: a stronger stimulus fires more neurons and more often, not a bigger spike.
The refractory period limits how soon a neuron can fire again and keeps the impulse travelling in one direction.
Myelin insulates the axon; the impulse jumps between nodes, which is why myelinated fibres conduct faster.
Neurotransmitters cross the synapse; agonists increase and antagonists block their effect; reuptake and enzymes end the signal.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors work by slowing reuptake, leaving more transmitter available in the synapse.

lesson.title: From resting potential to a drug in the synapse
objectives: Trace a signal from dendrite to synapse and name each structure's job.
Explain the all-or-none principle and what stimulus strength actually changes.
Describe how myelin, the refractory period and the synapse shape transmission.
Predict the effect of an agonist, an antagonist or a reuptake inhibitor.

body.text: The neuron is a cable that runs on chemistry at both ends and electricity in the middle. Nothing here is metaphorical — the exam asks you to be precise about which part is which.
The electrical half

At rest, a neuron holds a negative charge inside relative to outside, maintained by pumps and by the membrane being far more permeable to potassium than to sodium. Stimulation opens channels; enough positive charge flowing in reaches a **threshold**, and an action potential fires. Below threshold, nothing happens at all.

body.label: All-or-none
body.expression: stimulus below threshold → no action potential;  stimulus at or above threshold → full action potential, always the same size

body.label: The point students lose
body.text: A stronger stimulus does **not** produce a taller action potential. Intensity is coded by **how many** neurons fire and **how often** they fire. If an answer choice says 'a larger action potential', it is wrong.

Immediately after firing, the neuron is briefly unable to fire again — the **refractory period** — which also keeps the impulse moving away from the cell body rather than backwards. **Myelin** wraps the axon in insulating segments; the impulse leaps from node to node, which is far faster than continuous conduction, and damage to myelin slows or blocks signals.
The chemical half

When the impulse reaches the terminal buttons, vesicles release **neurotransmitter** into the synaptic gap. Molecules bind to receptors on the receiving neuron, opening channels that push it toward or away from its own threshold. The signal ends by **reuptake** into the sending neuron, by enzymatic breakdown, or by diffusion.

head: Agent
Mechanism
Net effect
rows: slows chemical breakdown of the transmitter

body.label: Apply it
body.text: An SSRI blocks the reuptake of serotonin. It does not create serotonin and does not bind the postsynaptic receptor as an agonist — it simply keeps the serotonin that was already released in the gap for longer. Predicting that mechanism is the whole question.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Confusing **excitatory** with **agonist**. Excitatory and inhibitory describe what a transmitter does at the receiving cell. Agonist and antagonist describe whether a drug increases or blocks a transmitter's action. An agonist of an inhibitory transmitter increases inhibition.

vocabulary.definition: The brief reversal of charge that travels along an axon once threshold is reached.
The level of depolarisation required to trigger an action potential.
The brief interval after firing during which a neuron cannot fire again.
Fatty insulation along an axon that speeds conduction by allowing the impulse to jump between nodes.
The junction where a sending neuron communicates with a receiving cell by chemical means.
Reabsorption of a neurotransmitter by the sending neuron, ending its action.
A drug that increases / blocks the action of a neurotransmitter.

formulas.label: Intensity coding
formulas.expression: stronger stimulus → more neurons firing and a higher firing rate, never a larger action potential

mistakes: Saying a stronger stimulus produces a larger action potential.
Treating the refractory period only as a limit on rate, when it also enforces one-way travel.
Calling every drug that boosts a transmitter an agonist, including reuptake inhibitors.
Forgetting that an agonist of an inhibitory transmitter produces more inhibition.
review: What does stimulus intensity change, if not the size of the action potential?
Why does myelination speed conduction?
How does an SSRI differ in mechanism from a serotonin agonist?

questions.prompt: A researcher doubles the intensity of a stimulus applied to a sensory neuron already firing above threshold. What happens?
choices: Each action potential becomes twice as large.
The action potential travels in both directions.
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none, so amplitude is fixed. Intensity is coded by firing rate and by the number of neurons recruited.

questions.prompt: A drug blocks the transporter that returns dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. What is the expected effect?
choices: Less dopamine in the synapse, because release is blocked.
Dopamine receptors on the receiving neuron are blocked.
More dopamine remains in the synapse for longer, prolonging its effect.
Dopamine is broken down faster by enzymes.
questions.explanation: Blocking reuptake leaves released dopamine in the gap longer, so its effect is prolonged. Release, receptor binding and enzymatic breakdown are untouched.

questions.prompt: Name the structure that speeds conduction by allowing the impulse to move between gaps in the insulation.
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, and the impulse jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — which is much faster than continuous conduction.

topics.title: The Brain
topics.summary: Structures and their functions, how imaging and lesion studies reveal them, and how the brain reorganises itself.
keyIdeas: Brainstem (medulla, pons) handles survival functions; the cerebellum coordinates movement and non-verbal learning.
The limbic system includes the amygdala (fear, aggression), hippocampus (new explicit memories) and hypothalamus (drives, hormones, reward).
Four cerebral lobes: frontal (planning, judgement, motor cortex), parietal (somatosensory), occipital (vision), temporal (audition, language comprehension).
Broca's area supports speech production; Wernicke's area supports comprehension.
Split-brain research shows that information presented to one visual field is processed by the opposite hemisphere.
Methods differ in what they buy: lesion and TMS studies show necessity, fMRI and PET show correlates, EEG has millisecond resolution but poor localisation.
Neuroplasticity allows functions to reorganise after damage; neurogenesis is limited and region-specific.

lesson.title: Brain structures, and what each method can actually show
objectives: Match a structure to its function and recognise the deficit that follows damage to it.
Explain lateralisation and what split-brain findings demonstrate.
Choose the right imaging or intervention method for a research question and justify the choice.
Describe evidence for plasticity and its limits.

body.text: Two skills are tested here: knowing what a structure does, and knowing what a method can prove. The second one separates the top scores.
Structures worth memorising in pairs

head: Structure
If it works
If it is damaged
rows: clumsy, uncoordinated movement; impaired non-verbal learning
reduced fear conditioning and threat detection
cannot form new explicit memories; older ones may survive
disturbed hunger, thirst, temperature and hormonal control
halting, effortful speech with intact comprehension
fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension

body.label: The classic case
body.text: Patient H.M. had his hippocampi removed to control epilepsy. He could hold a conversation and learn new motor skills, but could not form new explicit memories. That dissociation — procedural learning intact, explicit memory gone — is why the hippocampus is tied to forming new explicit memories rather than to 'memory' in general.
Lateralisation without overclaiming

Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, and each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere. In split-brain patients, whose corpus callosum has been severed, an object shown to the left visual field can be picked up with the left hand but not named, because the language areas sit in the other hemisphere.

body.label: Do not overclaim
body.text: 'Left-brained people are logical' is not a finding. Lateralisation means some functions are stronger in one hemisphere for most people; healthy brains integrate constantly, and individual differences are far smaller than the pop-psychology version suggests.
Method matching

head: Question you want answered
Best method
Why
rows: Is this region necessary for the behaviour?
removing or disrupting the region tests necessity
Which regions are active during the task?
good spatial resolution, non-invasive, but correlational and slow
When exactly does the response occur?

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Answering 'fMRI' when the question asks whether a region is **necessary**. Imaging shows what is active while something happens; only disruption or damage can show that the activity is required.

**Neuroplasticity** is the payoff concept: after injury, neighbouring regions and even the opposite hemisphere can take over some functions, most readily in children. Constraint-induced therapy and recovery after stroke are the standard evidence. Plasticity is real and substantial; it is not unlimited.

vocabulary.definition: The fibre bundle connecting the two hemispheres; severed in split-brain surgery.
The tendency for some functions to be stronger in one hemisphere.
The brain's capacity to reorganise structure and function in response to experience or injury.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation: temporarily disrupts or enhances a region, testing necessity.
Functional MRI: measures blood-oxygen changes to localise activity; correlational.
Event-related potential from EEG: precise timing of brain responses, imprecise location.

mistakes: Choosing an imaging method when the question asks about necessity.
Saying the hippocampus stores all long-term memory rather than being needed to form new explicit memories.
Repeating pop-psychology left/right-brain personality claims.
Treating plasticity as unlimited recovery.
review: Which method answers 'is this region necessary?' and why can't fMRI?
Why can a split-brain patient hold an object seen in the left visual field but not name it?
What did patient H.M. show about procedural versus explicit memory?

questions.prompt: A patient speaks fluently and grammatically, but the sentences carry little meaning and she cannot follow spoken instructions. Damage is most likely in which area?
questions.explanation: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is the signature of Wernicke's area damage. Broca's damage gives effortful, halting speech with comprehension preserved.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to know whether the right parietal cortex is necessary for a spatial attention task. Which method is most appropriate?
choices: fMRI while participants perform the task
TMS applied over the right parietal cortex during the task
A structural MRI comparison between high and low scorers
questions.explanation: Disrupting a region tests necessity. fMRI, EEG and structural MRI can only show what is active or present — correlates, not causes.

topics.title: Sleep
topics.summary: Stages and cycles, why we sleep, what disrupts it, and what happens when we do not get enough.
keyIdeas: Cycles of about 90 minutes alternate N1, N2, N3 and REM across the night; deep sleep dominates early, REM later.
N3 slow-wave sleep is hardest to wake from; vivid dreaming is most common in REM.
Circadian rhythms are entrained by light through the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which regulates melatonin.
Theories of sleep's function include restoration, memory consolidation, energy conservation and protection.
Disorders include insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea, night terrors, sleepwalking and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
Deprivation impairs attention, learning, consolidation, mood and immune function, and can produce microsleeps.

lesson.title: Sleep architecture, and the disorders that map onto it
objectives: Identify the sleep stages and what distinguishes them.
Explain how circadian rhythms are set and how they are disrupted.
Match a sleep disorder to the stage or mechanism it involves.
State the effects of sleep deprivation and the leading theories of sleep's function.

body.text: Sleep questions reward structure. Learn the cycle once, and most items become pattern matching.
The architecture

head: Stage
Signature
Notes
rows: brief; easy to wake; may include the sensation of falling
the largest share of a normal adult night
hardest to wake from; growth hormone release; night terrors and sleepwalking occur here
rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, muscle atonia
longer in the second half of the night; most dreaming reported here

body.label: The discrimination the exam loves
body.text: **Night terrors** occur in N3, mostly in children, and are rarely remembered. **Nightmares** occur in REM, are vividly remembered, and are common at any age. Pick the right one and the item is over.
Rhythms

Light detected by the retina signals the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, which adjusts the pineal gland's release of **melatonin**. This is why bright evening light delays sleepiness, why jet lag resolves in the direction of light exposure, and why shift work is genuinely hard on health.
Why sleep at all

items: **Restoration**: tissue repair and growth hormone release during deep sleep.
**Memory consolidation**: sleep after learning improves retention; REM and slow-wave sleep support different kinds of memory.
**Conservation and protection**: reduced energy use and reduced exposure during the most vulnerable hours.

body.text: What deprivation costs

Attention lapses and **microsleeps**, slower reaction time, worse encoding and worse consolidation, irritability and low mood, impaired immune response, and — with total deprivation — hallucinations and disorientation. A driver who feels 'fine' after short sleep is a poor judge of their own impairment, which is itself a deprivation effect.

body.label: Apply it
body.text: A student studies all night and reports 'knowing' the material the next morning. Predict the exam result and justify it: encoding may have succeeded, but consolidation depends on sleep, and the state in which she takes the test is depleted — so performance is likely to understate what was learned.

vocabulary.definition: An approximately 24-hour biological cycle, set largely by light.
Hypothalamic clock that responds to light and regulates melatonin release.
Hormone released by the pineal gland in darkness, promoting sleepiness.
Muscle paralysis during REM that prevents acting out dreams.
Sudden, uncontrollable entry into REM-like sleep during waking.
Repeated airway obstruction during sleep causing brief arousals and fragmented sleep.
A few seconds of involuntary sleep, typical of deprivation.

mistakes: Confusing night terrors (N3, unremembered) with nightmares (REM, vividly remembered).
Assuming most dreaming happens in N3 rather than REM.
Treating melatonin as a sleep hormone that causes sleep rather than one that signals darkness and promotes sleepiness.
Underestimating deprivation effects on consolidation rather than only on alertness.
review: Which stage contains sleep spindles, and which contains most reported dreaming?
How does light control melatonin release?
Why might all-night studying produce worse results than the student's familiarity suggests?

questions.prompt: A seven-year-old bolts upright screaming an hour after falling asleep, cannot be comforted, and has no memory of the event the next morning. This is most consistent with which?
questions.explanation: Night terrors occur in N3 early in the night, are common in children, resist comforting and are rarely remembered. Nightmares occur in REM, later in the night, and are vividly recalled.

questions.prompt: A traveller flying east several time zones finds it hardest to stay awake in the evening and wakes far too early. Which intervention targets the underlying rhythm?
choices: Timed bright light exposure in the morning
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is entrained by light, so timed morning light shifts the circadian phase. Caffeine and naps mask sleepiness without shifting the rhythm, and long naps reduce night-time sleep pressure.

questions.prompt: Name the hypothalamic structure that receives light information and acts as the body's clock.
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus receives retinal input and regulates melatonin release from the pineal gland, setting the circadian rhythm.

topics.title: Sensation
topics.summary: Transduction, thresholds, adaptation, and why detecting a stimulus is a decision and not a reading.
keyIdeas: Transduction converts physical energy into neural signals; each system has its own receptors.
Absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus detected half the time; the difference threshold is the smallest detectable change.
Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original intensity, not a fixed amount.
Sensory adaptation reduces sensitivity to unchanging stimulation.
Signal detection theory: detection depends on sensitivity and on the observer's criterion, motivation and expectations.
Subliminal stimulation may prime briefly but does not produce powerful hidden persuasion.

questions.prompt: A participant can just notice adding 5 g to a 100 g weight. According to Weber's law, roughly how much must be added to a 200 g weight to be just noticeable?
questions.explanation: Weber's law says the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion. 5 g of 100 g is 5%, so 5% of 200 g is 10 g.

questions.prompt: In a hearing test, a participant who is anxious about missing tones reports hearing faint sounds that are not there. Signal detection theory describes this as which?
choices: A lower absolute threshold caused by anxiety
A more liberal response criterion, producing more false alarms
questions.explanation: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity from the decision rule. Willingness to say 'yes' increases hits and false alarms together; the ear has not become more sensitive.

units.title: Cognition
units.summary: Perception, thinking and judgement, and the whole memory system — encoding, storage, retrieval, and how it fails.

topics.title: Perception
topics.summary: How the brain turns sensation into an organised, stable, meaningful world — and why it is sometimes wrong.
keyIdeas: Bottom-up processing builds from features; top-down processing applies expectations and context.
Gestalt principles: figure–ground, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure.
Depth cues are binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) or monocular (interposition, relative size, linear perspective, texture gradient, relative height and motion).
Perceptual constancy keeps size, shape, colour and brightness stable as conditions change.
Perceptual set and context shape what we see; illusions are systematic, not random errors.
Perceptual adaptation shows perception adjusts to changed input, such as inverting lenses.

questions.prompt: A row of dots is seen as two groups rather than one because the spacing between some of them is larger. Which principle explains this?
questions.explanation: Proximity groups elements that are near each other. Closure completes incomplete figures, continuity follows smooth lines, and figure–ground separates an object from its background.

questions.prompt: A car drives away and its image on the retina shrinks, yet you perceive it as the same size moving off. Which concept is at work?
questions.explanation: Size constancy maintains perceived size despite changes in retinal image size, using distance information. The other options are depth cues or a change in sensitivity.

topics.title: Thinking, Problem-Solving, Judgments, and Decision-Making
topics.summary: Concepts, prototypes, heuristics, and the biases that make judgement fast and predictably wrong.
keyIdeas: Algorithms guarantee a solution; heuristics are fast and usually good enough.
Availability: judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind.
Representativeness: judge category membership by similarity to a prototype, ignoring base rates.
Confirmation bias seeks confirming evidence; belief perseverance survives disproof; overconfidence inflates accuracy.
Framing changes decisions with identical outcomes; the overjustification of 'loss aversion' makes losses weigh more heavily than equivalent gains.
Functional fixedness and mental sets block creative problem solving; incubation and restructuring relieve them.

questions.prompt: After seeing three news reports about plane crashes, a traveller decides flying is far more dangerous than driving. Which heuristic is most at work?
questions.explanation: Vivid, easily recalled examples inflate judged frequency — availability. Representativeness would be judging by similarity to a stereotype instead.

questions.prompt: A participant is told a person is quiet, orderly and detail-oriented, then asked whether she is more likely a librarian or a salesperson. Ignoring that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians is which error?
choices: Ignoring base rates in favour of representativeness
questions.explanation: Judging by resemblance to a prototype while neglecting prior probabilities is the classic representativeness-plus-base-rate error.

topics.title: Introduction to Memory
topics.summary: The architecture: sensory registers, working memory, long-term memory, and the distinction between explicit and implicit.
keyIdeas: Atkinson–Shiffrin: sensory memory → short-term store → long-term store, with rehearsal moving information along.
Working memory (Baddeley) is not a passive buffer: it manipulates information, with phonological, visuospatial and executive components.
Long-term memory divides into explicit (episodic, semantic) and implicit (procedural, priming, conditioning).
Capacity of short-term memory is small; chunking expands it by recoding.
Amnesia can be anterograde (cannot form new explicit memories) or retrograde (loss of memories before the event).
Implicit memory can survive damage that destroys explicit memory.

questions.prompt: A patient with hippocampal damage learns a new mirror-tracing skill over several days but denies having practised it before. This shows that which?
choices: Procedural memory can be intact while explicit memory fails
Rehearsal is unnecessary for explicit memory
questions.explanation: Skill learning is implicit and depends on other structures; the inability to report having practised reflects the explicit-memory deficit. Retrograde amnesia would be loss of memories formed before the damage.

topics.title: Encoding Memories
topics.summary: Getting information in: attention, levels of processing, and the study habits that follow from the evidence.
keyIdeas: Encoding can be automatic or effortful; effortful encoding needs attention.
Levels of processing: semantic encoding beats acoustic, which beats visual.
The spacing effect: distributed practice outperforms massed practice for the same total time.
The testing effect: retrieving information strengthens it more than re-reading.
Elaboration, self-reference, and organising material into meaningful groups improve encoding.
Serial position: primacy reflects transfer to long-term storage, recency reflects the short-term store.

questions.prompt: Two students spend four hours each preparing. One reads the chapter four times; the other reads once and spends the rest self-testing. Which is better supported, and by which effect?
choices: Re-reading, by the serial position effect
Neither; total time is all that matters
questions.explanation: Retrieval practice produces better retention than re-exposure to the same material — the testing effect. The spacing effect favours spreading the same four hours across days, which is compatible but a different point.

topics.title: Storing Memories
topics.summary: What keeps a memory available: consolidation, organisation, and the biology that supports it.
keyIdeas: Consolidation stabilises memories over time and depends on sleep and on the hippocampus early on.
Memories are organised by meaning and by association, not stored as intact recordings.
Long-term potentiation in synaptic transmission is the leading cellular account of memory formation.
Stress hormones can strengthen emotionally significant memories while impairing accuracy of peripheral detail.
Reconsolidation: recalled memories can be altered before being stored again.

questions.prompt: A witness to a frightening event recalls the weapon in sharp detail but misremembers faces and the sequence of events. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Arousal narrows attention to the central, threatening detail at the cost of peripheral accuracy
questions.explanation: High arousal focuses encoding on the source of threat, which improves central detail and degrades peripheral detail. Interference and biological failure do not explain this selective pattern.

topics.title: Retrieving Memories
topics.summary: Getting information back out: cues, context, and why recognition is easier than recall.
keyIdeas: Retrieval cues trigger recall; more and better-matched cues help.
Context-dependent and state-dependent memory: retrieval is easier when the context or internal state matches encoding.
Recognition is easier than recall because the item itself acts as a cue.
Priming is the automatic activation of associated representations.
Tip-of-the-tongue states reflect partial retrieval, not absence of the memory.

questions.prompt: Name the phenomenon in which material learned in a particular room is remembered better back in that room.
questions.explanation: Retrieval is easier when the external context at recall matches the context at encoding — context-dependent memory, an instance of encoding specificity.

topics.title: Forgetting and Other Memory Challenges
topics.summary: Why memories fail, how suggestion reshapes them, and how the failures are distinguished on an exam.
keyIdeas: Encoding failure: the information was never stored — the most common everyday 'forgetting'.
Storage decay and retrieval failure are distinct; the memory may be available but inaccessible.
Proactive interference: old learning disrupts new. Retroactive interference: new learning disrupts old.
The misinformation effect: post-event information alters recollection.
Source amnesia: remembering content but not where it came from; a basis for unintentional plagiarism and false familiarity.
Motivated forgetting and repression remain contested; false memories can be implanted by suggestion.
The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: rapid early loss that then levels off.

lesson.title: Four ways to forget, and how to tell them apart
objectives: Classify a forgetting scenario as encoding failure, decay, interference or retrieval failure.
Distinguish proactive from retroactive interference in either direction.
Explain the misinformation effect and source amnesia with evidence.
Evaluate a claim about recovered memories using what the research supports.

body.text: Almost every forgetting item on this exam is a **classification** problem. Learn the four categories and the discriminating question for each.

head: Kind
Discriminating question
Example
rows: Was it ever attended to and stored?
You cannot recall the pattern on a coin you have used for years
Did the trace fade with disuse over time?
A language unused since childhood becomes inaccessible
Is the memory there but unreachable without the right cue?
Tip-of-the-tongue; the name returns later unprompted
You enter a room and forget why, because the new context displaced the intention

body.label: Interference direction
body.text: **Proactive** = old interferes with new (your previous address intrudes when you write the new one). **Retroactive** = new interferes with old (learning the new address makes the old one hard to recall). Ask which memory you are trying to retrieve and which is intruding: the intruder's age names the type.
Memory is reconstructive

Loftus showed that the wording of a question changes what people report: participants who heard 'smashed' estimated higher speeds and more often reported broken glass that was never there. Later information is not merely added — it becomes part of the memory. **Source amnesia** is the related failure: the content is retained, the origin is not, which is why a rumour can come to feel like a first-hand memory.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Writing 'memory works like a video recording that can be corrupted'. Say instead that memory is reconstructive: each recall rebuilds the event from fragments plus expectations, which is exactly why suggestion can alter it.
The contested claim

Traumatic memories can be intrusive and can also be delayed in their full impact; that much is well supported. The stronger claim — that accurate memories of abuse can be repressed and then recovered intact in therapy — is not well supported, and suggestive therapeutic techniques have demonstrably produced false memories in both laboratory and clinical settings. The exam rewards the distinction, not a verdict in either direction.

vocabulary.definition: Previously learned material disrupts recall of newly learned material.
Newly learned material disrupts recall of previously learned material.
Incorporating misleading post-event information into a memory of the event.
Retaining content while losing memory of where it came from.
Information never entered long-term storage because it was not attended to or processed.
Ebbinghaus's finding that forgetting is rapid at first and then levels off.

mistakes: Reversing proactive and retroactive interference.
Attributing everyday forgetting to decay when the usual cause is encoding failure.
Describing memory as a recording rather than a reconstruction.
Conflating delayed recall of trauma with evidence for accurate repressed and recovered memories.
review: Which kind of forgetting is behind failing to recall a detail you never attended to?
You keep writing your old password into a new form. Proactive or retroactive?
How does the wording of a question change a witness's report?

questions.prompt: A student who learned Spanish in high school now struggles to recall French vocabulary learned this year. This is which?
questions.explanation: The older Spanish is intruding on the newer French, which is proactive interference. If the new French were displacing recall of the Spanish, it would be retroactive.

questions.prompt: Witnesses asked whether they saw 'the broken headlight' are more likely to report one than witnesses asked about 'a broken headlight', even when there was none. Which effect does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Post-event wording supplied a detail that witnesses incorporated into the memory — the misinformation effect, evidence that memory is reconstructive.

topics.title: Intelligence and Achievement
topics.summary: What intelligence tests measure, how they are validated, and the arguments about bias and heritability.
keyIdeas: Spearman's g as a general factor; Gardner's multiple intelligences; Sternberg's triarchic theory.
Fluid intelligence (novel reasoning) declines with age; crystallised knowledge does not.
Tests are standardised against norms; a score's meaning comes from the comparison group.
Reliability is consistency; validity is measuring what the test claims to measure — including predictive validity.
The Flynn effect: scores rose across the twentieth century, which argues against a purely genetic reading.
Stereotype threat can depress performance in a testing situation.
Test bias debates concern both content and predictive fairness; achievement tests measure learned content, aptitude tests predict learning.

questions.prompt: A test predicts first-year university grades equally well for two groups, but the mean scores differ. Under a predictive-validity standard, the test is best described as which?
choices: Unbiased on this standard, because it predicts equally well for both groups
questions.explanation: Predictive validity asks whether the test forecasts the criterion equally well across groups. A mean difference is not, by itself, evidence of bias on that standard — though content bias and access are separate questions.

questions.prompt: Which best explains the Flynn effect?
choices: A rapid genetic change in the population over a few generations
Environmental changes such as schooling, nutrition and cognitively demanding environments
A statistical error in early norms
questions.explanation: Score gains over decades are far too fast for genetic change and too broad to be an artefact, so environmental change is the standard explanation — which is also why the effect complicates purely genetic accounts of group differences.

units.title: Development and Learning
units.summary: How people change across the lifespan, and the mechanisms — conditioning, observation, language — by which they learn.

topics.title: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology
topics.summary: Continuity and stages, stability and change, and the designs used to study development.
keyIdeas: Continuity versus stages: is development gradual or marked by qualitative shifts?
Stability versus change: which traits persist across the lifespan?
Nature and nurture interact throughout development; sensitive and critical periods differ in rigidity.
Cross-sectional designs compare age groups at one time — fast, but confounded by cohort effects.
Longitudinal designs follow one cohort over time — informative, but slow, costly and exposed to attrition.
Teratogens and prenatal environment shape development before birth.

questions.prompt: A study compares the memory performance of 20-year-olds and 70-year-olds tested today and concludes that memory declines with age. What is the main weakness?
choices: Cohort effects: the groups differ in education, health and experience as well as age
The study is longitudinal and therefore unreliable
questions.explanation: This is a cross-sectional design, so any difference could reflect the generations the groups grew up in rather than ageing itself. A longitudinal design would follow one cohort but is exposed to attrition.

topics.title: Physical Development Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Prenatal development, motor milestones, and the physical changes of adolescence, adulthood and ageing.
keyIdeas: Prenatal sequence: zygote, embryo, fetus; teratogens such as alcohol cause lasting damage.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Motor milestones follow a cephalocaudal and proximodistal sequence, with individual variation in timing.
Adolescent brain development: the limbic system matures ahead of the prefrontal cortex, which helps explain risk-taking.
Ageing brings declines in fluid abilities and sensory acuity, with stability or growth in crystallised knowledge.
Menopause, and the distinction between normal ageing and neurocognitive disorder.

questions.prompt: Which best explains why adolescents take more physical risks than adults, despite knowing the risks?
choices: They have not learned what the risks are
The limbic system matures earlier than the prefrontal cortex, so reward sensitivity outpaces inhibitory control
questions.explanation: Reward and emotion systems develop ahead of the prefrontal control system, so knowledge of risk does not translate into control under arousal. It is a developmental mismatch, not ignorance.

topics.title: Gender and Sexual Orientation
topics.summary: How gender identity, gender roles and sexual orientation develop, and how biology and culture each contribute.
keyIdeas: Sex is biological; gender identity is a person's sense of being male, female, both, neither or another gender.
Gender roles and stereotypes are culturally shaped and vary across time and place.
Gender typing emerges early and is influenced by biology, cognition and socialisation together.
Gender schema theory: children organise information by category and adjust behaviour to fit it.
Sexual orientation is not a choice and is not produced by parenting style; it is stable for most people.
Prejudice against gender-nonconforming and LGBTQ+ people is a social phenomenon with measurable health effects.

questions.prompt: A child insists that trucks are 'for boys' and refuses to play with one, having learned the category early. Which theory best accounts for this?
questions.explanation: Gender schema theory holds that children build categories for gender and then filter information and behaviour to fit them.

topics.title: Cognitive Development Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Piaget's stages and what later research revised, Vygotsky's social account, and theory of mind.
keyIdeas: Piaget: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational; schemas, assimilation, accommodation.
Object permanence emerges in the sensorimotor stage; conservation in the concrete operational stage; abstract and hypothetical reasoning in formal operations.
Egocentrism in the preoperational stage limits perspective taking.
Later research shows competencies appear earlier than Piaget proposed, and stage boundaries are softer.
Vygotsky: the zone of proximal development and scaffolding — learning is social before it is individual.
Theory of mind — understanding that others have different beliefs — develops in early childhood and is tested by false-belief tasks.

questions.prompt: A child agrees that two identical glasses hold the same amount of water, then says the taller, narrower glass holds more after the water is poured. Which is missing?
questions.explanation: Conservation — understanding that quantity is unchanged by a change in appearance — is typically absent in the preoperational stage and present in concrete operations.

questions.prompt: A teacher gives a student a problem just beyond what she can solve alone, then withdraws support as she improves. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: Scaffolding within the zone of proximal development
questions.explanation: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the range of tasks a learner can do with help, and scaffolding is the graduated support provided there.

topics.title: Communication and Language Development
topics.summary: How language is acquired on a timetable, and the nativist–learning debate behind it.
keyIdeas: Sequence: babbling → one-word → two-word → telegraphic speech → full syntax, with striking cross-cultural regularity.
Chomsky: an innate language acquisition device and universal grammar; poverty of the stimulus.
Learning accounts: imitation, reinforcement and statistical learning from input.
A critical or sensitive period: language acquired late, after severe deprivation, is rarely fully acquired.
Whorf's linguistic determinism in its strong form is not supported; a weaker version — language influences thought — has some support.
Receptive language develops ahead of productive language.

questions.prompt: Children across unrelated languages produce similar babbling and pass through the same one-word and two-word stages, and they generate sentences they have never heard. Which position does this most support?
choices: Language is learned entirely by imitation and reinforcement
Humans have a biological preparedness for language acquisition
Language shapes thought in a deterministic way
Language is acquired only after age seven
questions.explanation: Universal sequences plus novel, unimitated productions are the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument for an innate capacity. Imitation alone cannot explain productivity.

topics.title: Social-Emotional Development Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Attachment, temperament, parenting, moral development and identity across the lifespan.
keyIdeas: Harlow's surrogate-mother studies showed contact comfort matters beyond feeding.
Ainsworth's Strange Situation classifies attachment as secure, avoidant or resistant; disorganised was added later.
Attachment patterns relate to caregiver sensitivity and predict later social functioning, without determining it.
Temperament is biologically based and observable early; it interacts with parenting.
Baumrind's styles: authoritative (high demand, high warmth) is most consistently associated with competence; authoritarian, permissive and neglectful fare worse.
Kohlberg's moral stages (preconventional, conventional, postconventional) and Gilligan's care-oriented critique.
Erikson's psychosocial stages run across the whole lifespan, from trust to integrity.

questions.prompt: In the Strange Situation, an infant explores freely with the caregiver present, is distressed at separation and is quickly comforted on return. This pattern is which?
questions.explanation: Secure attachment uses the caregiver as a safe base: exploration when present, protest at departure, easy comfort on return. Avoidant infants show little distress; resistant infants are not easily soothed.

questions.prompt: Parents set clear, consistently enforced expectations, explain the reasons behind them and are responsive to the child's perspective. Which style is this?
questions.explanation: Authoritative parenting combines high demandingness with high warmth. Authoritarian is high demand with low warmth; permissive is warmth without demands.

topics.title: Classical Conditioning
topics.summary: Learning by association: what the elements are, how the association changes, and how it is used clinically.
keyIdeas: Unconditioned stimulus produces an unconditioned response; a neutral stimulus paired with it becomes a conditioned stimulus producing a conditioned response.
Acquisition builds the association; extinction weakens it when the CS is presented alone.
Spontaneous recovery shows extinction suppresses rather than erases the association.
Generalisation spreads the response to similar stimuli; discrimination narrows it.
Higher-order conditioning pairs a new CS with an established one.
Taste aversion can form after a single pairing with a long delay — an exception to standard contingency rules.
Applications: counterconditioning, systematic desensitisation, aversion therapy, and the conditioned component of drug cues and immunity.

lesson.title: Identifying the four elements, every time
objectives: Label US, UR, CS and CR in any scenario.
Explain acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination.
Account for taste aversion as a genuine exception to standard rules.
Describe clinical applications such as systematic desensitisation.

body.text: Every classical conditioning item is solved the same way. Find the reflex first, then find the signal.
The four elements

head: Element
Test
In Pavlov's dogs
rows: produces the response automatically, before any learning
the automatic response to the US
a previously neutral stimulus that now predicts the US
the learned response to the CS

body.label: The trick that catches people
body.text: The UR and the CR often look identical — salivating either way. They are different responses with different causes. The UR is unlearned and triggered by the US; the CR is learned and triggered by the CS, and it is usually weaker and more anticipatory. If an answer calls the CR 'the same thing as the UR', read it carefully.
How the association changes

items: **Acquisition** strengthens as CS and US are paired, fastest with short, reliable, predictive pairings. Forward conditioning (CS first) works; backward conditioning barely does.
**Extinction**: repeated CS without US reduces the CR. Extinction is new learning, not erasure.
**Spontaneous recovery**: after a rest, the extinguished CR returns weakly — the direct evidence that extinction suppressed it.
**Generalisation**: similar stimuli elicit the response (Little Albert's fear spreading to other furry objects).
**Discrimination**: learning which similar stimuli do not predict the US.
**Higher-order conditioning**: a new neutral stimulus paired with an established CS becomes a CS itself, usually more weakly.

body.label: The exception worth memorising
body.text: Taste aversion forms after **one** pairing, tolerates a delay of **hours** between the taste and the illness, and is selective — nausea attaches to taste far more readily than to a sound or a light. Garcia's work showed that organisms are biologically prepared for some associations, which is why conditioning is not a single general-purpose law.
What it is used for

**Systematic desensitisation** pairs relaxation with a graded hierarchy of feared stimuli, counterconditioning the fear response. **Aversion therapy** pairs a stimulus with an unpleasant response. Conditioned cues also explain why drug-related contexts provoke craving, and why tolerance is partly situational.

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Calling the CS a 'reward'. Classical conditioning has no reward — the CS predicts something that already happens. Reward and consequence belong to operant conditioning. Mixing the two up is the single most common error in this unit.

vocabulary.definition: A stimulus that automatically produces a response, and that response.
A formerly neutral stimulus that now predicts the US, and the learned response it elicits.
Weakening of the CR when the CS is repeatedly presented without the US.
Reappearance of an extinguished CR after a rest period.
Responding to similar stimuli / learning not to respond to stimuli that do not predict the US.
Pairing a feared stimulus with a new, incompatible response such as relaxation.
The tendency to form some associations more easily than others because of evolutionary history.

mistakes: Calling the conditioned stimulus a reward.
Treating extinction as erasure rather than new inhibitory learning.
Forgetting that taste aversion breaks the one-trial and short-delay rules.
Confusing the CR with the UR because the behaviour looks the same.
review: In a scenario where a nurse's white coat predicts an injection, which is the CS and which is the CR?
Why does spontaneous recovery matter theoretically?
How does systematic desensitisation use counterconditioning?

questions.prompt: A patient feels anxious on entering a clinic waiting room where she previously received a painful injection. In classical conditioning terms, the waiting room is which?
questions.explanation: The waiting room was neutral and now predicts the painful injection, so it is the CS. The pain is the US, the anxiety is the CR, and nothing here is a reinforcer — that is operant conditioning.

questions.prompt: A conditioned fear response is extinguished, then returns weakly a week later with no further pairings. What does this show?
choices: Extinction suppressed the association rather than erasing it
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the classic evidence that extinction is new inhibitory learning layered over the original association, not deletion of it.

questions.prompt: A person becomes nauseated by a food eaten six hours before a stomach illness, but does not develop an aversion to the music playing at the time. Which principle does this illustrate?
choices: Biological preparedness: taste associates with nausea more readily than sound does
questions.explanation: Taste aversion forms after one trial, across long delays, and selectively for taste — evidence that organisms are prepared for some associations rather than learning any pairing equally.

topics.title: Operant Conditioning
topics.summary: Learning by consequence: reinforcement, punishment, schedules, and why the distinctions matter.
keyIdeas: Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it. Both come in positive (add) and negative (remove) forms.
Negative reinforcement is not punishment — removing something aversive to increase a behaviour.
Primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs; conditioned reinforcers gain value by association.
Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a target behaviour.
Schedules: fixed and variable, ratio and interval. Variable ratio produces the highest, most persistent responding and the strongest resistance to extinction.
Latent learning (Tolman) and intrinsic motivation show that behaviour is not only reinforcement-driven; the overjustification effect shows extrinsic rewards can undermine it.
Learned helplessness follows repeated uncontrollable aversive events.

lesson.title: Positive, negative, reinforcement, punishment — a method that never fails
objectives: Classify any consequence as positive/negative reinforcement or positive/negative punishment using a two-question method.
Predict behaviour from a reinforcement schedule.
Explain shaping, latent learning and the overjustification effect.
Evaluate why punishment is used despite its limitations.

body.text: Two questions, asked in this order, classify every scenario on the exam.

items: Did the behaviour **increase or decrease** afterwards? Increase → reinforcement. Decrease → punishment.
Was something **added or removed**? Added → positive. Removed → negative.

head: Something added
Something removed
rows: Negative reinforcement — a headache stops after taking a tablet
Positive punishment — a fine after speeding

body.label: The one everyone loses
body.text: Negative reinforcement **increases** behaviour by removing something unpleasant. Taking a painkiller is negatively reinforced; so is giving in to a child's whining, which is why the whining continues. It is never punishment.
Schedules

head: Schedule
Rule
Pattern
rows: high rate with a pause after reinforcement; piecework pay
reinforce after an unpredictable number of responses
highest, most persistent rate; very resistant to extinction; gambling
reinforce the first response after a set time
scalloped pattern; responding rises as the interval ends; weekly pay
reinforce the first response after an unpredictable time
steady, moderate rate; pop quizzes, checking a feed

body.text: If a question asks which schedule makes a behaviour hardest to extinguish, the answer is **variable ratio**. Unpredictability is what keeps responding going through long stretches without reward.
Beyond the box

items: **Shaping**: reinforce successive approximations, raising the criterion as the animal improves.
**Latent learning** (Tolman): rats explored a maze without reward and demonstrated the learning immediately once reward appeared — cognition, not just reinforcement.
**Overjustification effect**: rewarding an already intrinsically enjoyable activity can reduce later interest in it once the reward stops.
**Learned helplessness** (Seligman): after inescapable shock, animals failed to escape avoidable shock — uncontrollability, not pain, produced the deficit, and it models part of depression.

body.label: Why punishment underperforms
body.text: Punishment suppresses behaviour without teaching a replacement, produces fear and avoidance of the punisher, models aggression, and works only while it is delivered consistently. Reinforcing an incompatible alternative behaviour is usually the better answer on the exam and in practice.

vocabulary.definition: Increasing a behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus.
Decreasing a behaviour by presenting an aversive stimulus.
A neutral stimulus that gains reinforcing value through association, such as money or grades.
Reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behaviour.
Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses; highest and most persistent rate.
Learning that occurs without reinforcement and is demonstrated only when there is a reason to.
External rewards reducing intrinsic interest in an already enjoyable activity.
Passivity after repeated uncontrollable aversive events.

mistakes: Calling negative reinforcement punishment.
Confusing ratio with interval schedules — ratio counts responses, interval waits for time.
Assuming punishment teaches the correct behaviour rather than only suppressing the wrong one.
Forgetting that the overjustification effect runs the other way to standard reinforcement.
review: Apply the two questions to: a driver fastens a seatbelt to stop the warning chime.
Which schedule best explains persistent gambling?
Why is punishment a poor long-term strategy on its own?

questions.prompt: A student studies hard and her parents cancel her Saturday chores. Her studying increases. This is which?
questions.explanation: Something aversive was removed (the chores) and the behaviour increased — negative reinforcement. Nothing unpleasant was presented, so it is not punishment.

questions.prompt: Which schedule produces the highest, most persistent rate of responding and the greatest resistance to extinction?
questions.explanation: Unpredictable reinforcement after a variable number of responses keeps responding high through unrewarded stretches, which is why gambling machines are built on it.

questions.prompt: A child who loved drawing is given a reward for each picture. When the rewards stop, she draws less than before. This is which?
choices: Extinction of a classically conditioned response
questions.explanation: An external reward applied to an intrinsically motivated activity can displace the internal reason for doing it, so interest drops below baseline once the reward is withdrawn.

topics.title: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning
topics.summary: Observational learning, expectancies and self-efficacy, and the brain systems that make learning stick.
keyIdeas: Bandura's observational learning: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; modelling of prosocial and antisocial behaviour.
The Bobo doll studies showed imitation of aggression without direct reinforcement; vicarious reinforcement and punishment matter.
Reciprocal determinism: behaviour, cognition and environment each influence the others.
Self-efficacy — belief in one's capability — predicts persistence and performance.
Mirror neuron research suggests a neural basis for imitation, though its interpretation is contested.
Memory consolidation during sleep, the role of the hippocampus and dopamine-based reward prediction in learning.

questions.prompt: Children who watched an adult model attack a doll later imitated the aggression, having received no reinforcement themselves. Which account does this support?
choices: Learning requires direct reinforcement of the learner's own behaviour
Learning can occur through observation of a model and its consequences
questions.explanation: Bandura's Bobo doll studies demonstrated observational learning: the children acquired and reproduced the behaviour without being reinforced for it.

questions.prompt: Two students with equal skill approach a difficult exam. One believes she can handle it, the other doubts her capability. The first studies longer and persists after a setback. Which construct best captures the difference?
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is the belief in one's capability to succeed in a specific situation, and it predicts effort and persistence independently of actual skill.

units.title: Social Psychology and Personality
units.summary: How other people shape behaviour and belief, and how enduring individual differences are described and measured.

topics.title: Attribution Theory and Person Perception
topics.summary: How we explain behaviour, and the systematic errors we make while doing it.
keyIdeas: Dispositional attributions locate the cause in the person; situational attributions locate it in the context.
The fundamental attribution error: overestimating disposition and underestimating situation when explaining others.
Actor–observer difference: we explain our own behaviour more situationally than others do.
The self-serving bias takes credit for success and deflects blame for failure.
First impressions, the halo effect and implicit associations shape person perception, often outside awareness.
Culture moderates these errors: individualist cultures show stronger dispositional bias.

questions.prompt: A driver cut off in traffic concludes the other driver is a reckless person rather than considering a medical emergency. This is which?
questions.explanation: Attributing another's behaviour to disposition while neglecting situational pressure is the fundamental attribution error.

topics.title: Attitude Formation and Attitude Change
topics.summary: Where attitudes come from, how they are changed, and what happens when they clash with behaviour.
keyIdeas: Attitudes form through direct experience, socialisation, conditioning and observation.
Cognitive dissonance: inconsistency between attitude and behaviour produces discomfort, which people reduce by changing one or the other.
Festinger and Carlsmith: the $1 group rated a dull task more enjoyable than the $20 group, because insufficient justification forced an attitude change.
Persuasion runs through a central route (arguments, durable change) and a peripheral route (cues such as attractiveness and length of message).
The elaboration likelihood model predicts which route is used, based on motivation and ability to process.
Mere exposure increases liking; foot-in-the-door works by securing a small commitment first.
Attitudes predict behaviour best when they are specific, strongly held and formed by direct experience.

questions.prompt: Paid $1 to tell the next participant a boring task was fun, a person later reports enjoying it; a person paid $20 does not. Which explains the difference?
choices: The $1 group had insufficient external justification and so reduced dissonance by changing the attitude
The $1 group had a more favourable attitude before the study
questions.explanation: With little external justification for the lie, the $1 participants reduced the inconsistency between what they said and what they believed by convincing themselves the task was enjoyable.

topics.title: Psychology of Social Situations
topics.summary: Conformity, obedience, group performance, helping and aggression — the situational forces that override disposition.
keyIdeas: Asch's line studies: a substantial minority of responses conformed to an obviously wrong majority; unanimity and group size matter.
Milgram's obedience studies: a majority continued to the maximum shock under an authority's instruction; proximity and institutional context shifted the rate.
Deindividuation reduces self-awareness and restraint in crowds and online.
Groupthink: cohesion and pressure for agreement suppress dissent and produce poor decisions.
Group polarisation pushes a group's average position further in its initial direction; social facilitation improves performance on easy or well-learned tasks and impairs it on hard ones.
Social loafing: reduced effort when individual output cannot be identified.
Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility (Latané and Darley): more bystanders, slower help.
Aggression: frustration–aggression, modelling, media effects debates, and situational triggers such as heat and provocation.
Prejudice reduction: superordinate goals, contact under conditions of equal status, and the limits of each.

lesson.title: Conformity, obedience and helping: three studies, three mechanisms
objectives: Explain what Asch, Milgram and Latané and Darley each demonstrated and what varied the outcome.
Distinguish conformity, compliance and obedience.
Predict group performance from task type and identifiability.
Evaluate the ethics and the modern criticisms of these classic studies.

body.text: These three studies carry a disproportionate share of the exam. Learn the finding, the variable that changed it, and the criticism — that combination answers almost any question built on them.
Asch: conformity to a wrong majority

Participants judged line lengths alongside confederates who unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. About a third of the critical trials produced agreement with the majority, and most participants conformed at least once. Two variables mattered most: **unanimity** — a single dissenting ally collapsed conformity — and **group size**, which mattered up to about three and then flattened.

body.label: The detail that earns the point
body.text: When asked why they conformed, some participants reported doubting their own perception (informational influence) and others reported not wanting to stand out (normative influence). Naming both gives you the mechanism, not just the number.
Milgram: obedience to authority

Participants, told the study concerned learning, administered what they believed were escalating electric shocks to a learner on an experimenter's instruction. A majority continued to the highest level. Obedience fell when the learner was in the room, when the experimenter gave instructions by telephone, and when the study moved out of a prestigious institutional setting.

body.label: How to treat this study today
body.text: Milgram's study is a legitimate finding about situational pressure and a serious ethical failure at once: deception, no genuine right to withdraw, and real psychological distress. Modern replications with weaker, ethicalised procedures find broadly similar obedience, but the original cannot be repeated and should be described as historically important rather than as a template. Say both halves.
Latané and Darley: why nobody helps

Participants who believed others could also hear an emergency helped less and more slowly as the perceived number of bystanders grew. Two mechanisms: **diffusion of responsibility** — the obligation is spread thin — and **pluralistic ignorance** — nobody acts, so each takes everyone's calm as evidence that nothing is wrong.

body.label: Apply it
body.text: Someone collapses in a crowded station and nobody moves. Predict what single intervention is most likely to produce help: pointing at one person and giving a specific instruction. It removes both diffusion and ambiguity at once, which is exactly what the research predicts.
Groups: which way does performance go?

body.text: Writing that 'being in a group reduces performance'. It depends on identifiability and task type. A group with individually attributable output on a well-practised task can outperform individuals.

Agreeing to a request from someone without authority over you.
Following the instructions of a perceived authority.

Which two mechanisms explain the bystander effect?
