questions.prompt: In Asch's studies, conformity dropped sharply when which change was made?
choices: The task was made more difficult
One confederate gave the correct answer, breaking unanimity
The group size increased from three to ten
Participants were told the study was about vision
questions.explanation: Unanimity is what drives conformity; a single ally gives the participant permission to dissent. Increasing group size beyond about three has little further effect.

questions.prompt: A person collapses in a busy station and nobody helps. Which pair of mechanisms best explains this?
choices: Diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance
Fundamental attribution error and self-serving bias
questions.explanation: Responsibility is spread across bystanders, and each person's inaction reads to the others as evidence that nothing is wrong. Both are established components of the bystander effect.

questions.prompt: Which best states the ethical problem with Milgram's obedience studies?
choices: Participants were deceived and subjected to significant distress without a genuine opportunity to withdraw
The sample was too small to generalise
The dependent variable was not operationalised
questions.explanation: The core problems are deception about the true purpose and the shocks, substantial psychological distress, and pressure that undermined the right to withdraw. Sample size and measurement were not the central criticisms.

topics.title: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality
topics.summary: Freud's structural model and defences, the neo-Freudians, and the humanistic alternative.
keyIdeas: Id, ego and superego; the ego mediates between instinct, reality and conscience.
Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalisation, reaction formation, sublimation.
Psychosexual stages and fixation; the Oedipus complex.
Neo-Freudians shifted weight from drives to social and cultural forces: Adler (inferiority), Horney (anxiety), Jung (collective unconscious).
Humanistic theories: Rogers' self-concept, congruence and unconditional positive regard; Maslow's hierarchy and self-actualisation.
Both traditions are influential but weakly falsifiable, and projective tests such as the Rorschach have poor reliability and validity.

questions.prompt: A student who is furious with a professor instead shouts at her roommate. Which defence mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects an impulse toward a safer target. Projection would be attributing her own anger to someone else; sublimation would be channelling it into a socially valued activity.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest methodological criticism of psychodynamic theory?
choices: It relies too heavily on controlled experiments
Its central claims are difficult or impossible to falsify, and explanations can be constructed after the fact
questions.explanation: Any behaviour can be reinterpreted to fit the theory, which makes it hard to specify an observation that would refute it. That is the standard scientific criticism, distinct from any claim about its clinical value.

topics.title: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality
topics.summary: Describing personality with traits, predicting behaviour with cognitive processes, and measuring both.
keyIdeas: The Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) is the dominant empirically derived model.
Traits are relatively stable, heritable to a moderate degree, and predictive of real outcomes such as work performance and health.
Eysenck proposed fewer, biologically grounded dimensions.
Bandura's reciprocal determinism: person, behaviour and environment mutually influence one another.
Self-efficacy and expectancies shape which situations people enter and how they persist.
The person–situation debate: traits predict averages across situations; situations predict specific acts.
Objective inventories such as the MMPI use empirically derived items; self-report measures are open to impression management.

questions.prompt: A person high in which Big Five trait is most likely to meet deadlines consistently and plan ahead?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness covers self-discipline, orderliness and achievement striving, and it is one of the best trait predictors of job and academic performance.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds that a trait predicts a person's average behaviour across many situations but not what they do in any single one. This is consistent with which?
choices: The resolution of the person–situation debate: traits predict aggregates, situations predict single acts
questions.explanation: Aggregating across occasions reveals stable trait effects that single observations bury. This reconciles the debate rather than settling it for either side.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.summary: What directs and sustains behaviour: drives, incentives, needs, and the physiology of hunger and achievement.
keyIdeas: Drive-reduction theory: physiological need creates tension that behaviour reduces; homeostasis is the goal.
Incentive theory: behaviour is pulled by anticipated rewards, not only pushed by internal states.
Arousal theory and the Yerkes–Dodson law: moderate arousal optimises performance, lower for difficult tasks.
Maslow's hierarchy: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation — influential but not well supported as a strict sequence.
Self-determination: autonomy, competence and relatedness support intrinsic motivation.
Hunger involves ghrelin, leptin, glucose and hypothalamic circuits; set-point and body weight are regulated, not simply chosen.
Achievement motivation and the distinction between mastery and performance goals.

questions.prompt: A pianist performs well before a small audience but badly before a large one on a difficult new piece. Which principle explains this?
choices: The Yerkes–Dodson law: high arousal impairs performance on difficult tasks
questions.explanation: Optimal arousal is lower for complex or unfamiliar tasks, so the same audience that helps on a well-practised piece can disrupt a difficult one.

topics.title: Emotion
topics.summary: Theories of how emotion arises, the role of physiology and cognition, and how emotion is expressed and detected.
keyIdeas: James–Lange: physiological response first, then the feeling that follows from perceiving it.
Cannon–Bard: physiological arousal and subjective experience occur together and independently.
Schachter–Singer two-factor: arousal plus a cognitive label; the same arousal can be labelled differently depending on context.
Zajonc and LeDoux: some emotional responses occur rapidly without conscious appraisal.
Lazarus: cognitive appraisal is necessary even for the simplest emotion.
Facial expressions for basic emotions are recognised across cultures; facial feedback suggests expression influences feeling.
Polygraph measures arousal, not deception, so it produces false positives with anxious truthful people.

questions.prompt: A man's heart races after crossing a shaky bridge, and he attributes the arousal to attraction toward the woman who met him there. Which theory does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Two-factor theory holds that arousal must be cognitively labelled; misattributed arousal from the bridge was labelled as attraction, exactly as in Dutton and Aron's study.

questions.prompt: Name the theory that says we feel afraid because we notice our heart pounding.
questions.explanation: James–Lange proposes that the perception of physiological arousal constitutes the emotion; Cannon–Bard and two-factor theories disagree about whether cognition is needed.

units.title: Mental and Physical Health
units.summary: Stress and coping, positive psychology, and how psychological disorders are explained, classified and treated.

topics.title: Introduction to Health Psychology
topics.summary: Stress, appraisal, coping and the behaviours that carry most of the health risk.
keyIdeas: Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
Lazarus: stress depends on appraisal — whether a demand is seen as exceeding resources.
Stressors vary in type: catastrophes, major life changes and daily hassles, with daily hassles being a strong predictor.
Chronic stress elevates cortisol and suppresses immune function.
Coping is problem-focused or emotion-focused; effective coping depends on whether the situation is controllable.
Social support, exercise, sleep and perceived control buffer stress; the tend-and-befriend response complements fight-or-flight.
Health behaviour change follows models such as the transtheoretical stages of change.

questions.prompt: A student facing an unchangeable exam date decides to manage her anxiety rather than try to remove the stressor. Which coping style is this?
questions.explanation: Emotion-focused coping regulates the emotional response when the stressor itself cannot be changed. Problem-focused coping targets the source, which is the better fit when the situation is controllable.

topics.title: Positive Psychology
topics.summary: What makes life go well: strengths, meaning, flow, gratitude and resilience — studied empirically rather than assumed.
keyIdeas: Seligman's PERMA: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment.
Flow: absorption when challenge matches skill.
Character strengths and virtues as measurable dispositions, distinct from the absence of disorder.
Gratitude practice, savoring and self-compassion show measurable but modest effects.
Resilience is ordinary rather than exceptional — most people recover from adversity.
Limits: self-esteem inflation and forced positivity can backfire; effects are real but not transformational.

questions.prompt: A rock climber loses track of time on a route that is difficult but within her ability. Which concept best describes this state?
questions.explanation: Flow occurs when challenge and skill are closely matched, producing deep absorption. Tasks far above skill produce anxiety; far below produce boredom.

topics.title: Explaining and Classifying Psychological Disorders
topics.summary: What counts as a disorder, how classification works, and the competing explanations for why disorders arise.
keyIdeas: Disorder criteria include distress, impairment, deviance from norms and dysfunction — no single criterion is sufficient.
The DSM-5-TR classifies by symptom patterns; the ICD serves international and billing use.
Classification improves communication and research but risks over-pathologising and label effects.
Comorbidity is the rule, not the exception; transdiagnostic processes cut across categories.
Models: biological, psychological, sociocultural, and the biopsychosocial integration; diathesis–stress combines vulnerability with triggering experience.
Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' showed how labels bias interpretation of normal behaviour.
Culture shapes both expression and diagnosis; culture-bound presentations exist and diagnostic criteria carry cultural assumptions.

questions.prompt: A person carries a genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia that never produces symptoms because his environment is stable and low-stress. Which framework does this fit?
questions.explanation: Diathesis–stress holds that an underlying vulnerability produces disorder only when sufficient stress is present — neither factor alone is sufficient.

questions.prompt: Rosenhan's pseudopatients were admitted after reporting a single false symptom and then behaved normally. Staff continued to interpret their ordinary behaviour as pathological. What does this demonstrate?
choices: That diagnostic labels bias the interpretation of subsequent behaviour
That schizophrenia is not a real condition
questions.explanation: Once applied, a label became the lens through which the same behaviour was read — the danger of diagnostic labelling. The study does not show that the disorders themselves are unreal.

topics.title: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders
topics.summary: The major diagnostic categories: anxiety, OCD, trauma, mood, schizophrenia, dissociative, somatic, personality, neurodevelopmental and eating disorders.
keyIdeas: Anxiety disorders: generalised anxiety, panic disorder and specific phobias are distinguished by focus, timing and triggers.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: obsessions are intrusive thoughts, compulsions are the acts performed to neutralise them.
Post-traumatic stress disorder follows a traumatic event and includes intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions and arousal.
Major depressive disorder requires persistent low mood or anhedonia with additional symptoms; bipolar disorder adds manic or hypomanic episodes.

Schizophrenia: positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganisation) and negative symptoms (avolition, flat affect); dopamine hypotheses and diathesis–stress; expressed emotion predicts relapse.
Dissociative disorders include dissociative identity disorder, the most contested category in the DSM.
Somatic symptom disorder centres on distress about bodily symptoms.
Neurodevelopmental disorders include ADHD and autism spectrum disorder; earlier 'Asperger's' is subsumed into the spectrum.
Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder differ in restriction, compensation and weight.
Personality disorders are enduring, inflexible patterns; antisocial and borderline are the most frequently examined.
Symptoms in this content are described for study purposes only and are never a basis for self-diagnosis.

lesson.title: Separating the categories that look alike
objectives: Distinguish the anxiety disorders from one another and from OCD.
Separate major depression from bipolar disorder and from normal low mood.
Describe schizophrenia's positive and negative symptoms and the evidence behind them.
Distinguish the eating disorders by restriction, compensation and weight status.

body.label: Read this first
body.text: This topic describes diagnostic criteria for study. It is not clinical advice, and recognising a symptom in yourself is not a diagnosis. If something here is worrying you, talk to a qualified clinician or a trusted adult — that is a normal thing to do, not a sign of anything.
The exam does not ask you to recite criteria. It gives a vignette and asks which category fits, so the skill is **discrimination** between neighbours.
Anxiety, OCD, trauma

Distinguishing feature
rows: persistent, diffuse worry across many domains for months, hard to control
recurrent abrupt panic attacks plus worry about further attacks
immediate, disproportionate fear cued by a particular object or situation, actively avoided
intrusive unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive acts performed to reduce the distress they cause (compulsions)

body.label: The OCD discrimination
body.text: A compulsion is defined by its function: it is performed to neutralise anxiety or prevent a dreaded event, and it is experienced as excessive. A careful habit that the person enjoys and would be annoyed to lose is not a compulsion.
Mood disorders

**Major depressive disorder** requires persistent depressed mood or loss of interest, plus changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, worthlessness or thoughts of death, causing impairment. **Bipolar disorder** is defined by the presence of manic or hypomanic episodes — elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep, grandiosity and pressured activity — not by the depth of the depression. The single question that separates them: has there ever been a distinct period of abnormally elevated mood and energy?
Schizophrenia

**Positive symptoms** add something: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour. **Negative symptoms** subtract something: reduced expression, avolition, alogia, social withdrawal — and they predict long-term functioning better than the positive ones. The **dopamine hypothesis** links excess dopamine activity to positive symptoms and is the basis of typical antipsychotics; **diathesis–stress** explains onset; high **expressed emotion** in families predicts relapse.
Eating disorders

head: Disorder
Restriction
Compensatory behaviour
Typical weight
rows: may or may not be present

body.label: Common mistake
body.text: Assuming low weight is required for an eating disorder diagnosis. Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder occur across the weight range, and restricting behaviour without low weight still warrants attention. Body weight is not a measure of severity.
The contested one

Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct personality states with gaps in recall. It is genuinely contested: prevalence rose sharply after media coverage, diagnostic criteria changed over time, and clinicians disagree about how much is iatrogenic. The exam rewards stating that the controversy exists and what each side argues.

vocabulary.definition: An intrusive, unwanted thought, image or urge that causes distress.
A repetitive act performed to reduce the distress caused by an obsession.
A distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and reduced need for sleep.
A behaviour or experience added to normal functioning, such as a hallucination.
A reduction or loss of normal functioning, such as flat affect or avolition.
Critical, hostile or emotionally over-involved family communication that predicts relapse in schizophrenia.
The presence of two or more disorders in the same person at the same time.

mistakes: Confusing obsessions with compulsions, or calling any careful habit a compulsion.
Defining bipolar disorder by the severity of depression rather than by the presence of mania.
Assuming eating disorders require low body weight.
Treating dissociative identity disorder as settled rather than contested.
Using this content to diagnose oneself or other people.

What distinguishes a specific phobia from generalised anxiety disorder?
Why do negative symptoms matter more than positive ones for long-term outcome?

questions.prompt: A person checks the stove repeatedly each morning because an intrusive image of the house burning will not leave until he does. Which pairing is correct?
choices: The image is the compulsion; the checking is the obsession
The image is the obsession; the checking is the compulsion
questions.explanation: The intrusive, unwanted image is the obsession; the repetitive checking performed to neutralise the distress is the compulsion.

questions.prompt: A person reports several weeks of almost no sleep, rapid speech, grand plans and high energy, followed by weeks of low mood and fatigue. Which is most consistent with this pattern?
questions.explanation: The presence of a distinct manic or hypomanic episode is what defines bipolar disorder, regardless of how severe the depressive periods are.

questions.prompt: Which feature of schizophrenia best predicts long-term social and occupational functioning?
questions.explanation: Negative symptoms — avolition, flat affect, social withdrawal — track functional outcome more closely than positive symptoms, which respond better to medication.

topics.title: Treatment of Psychological Disorders
topics.summary: Insight, behavioural, cognitive and biomedical treatments; what the evidence supports; and how care is delivered and funded.
keyIdeas: Insight therapies: psychoanalysis, client-centred therapy (Rogers), and psychodynamic approaches aim at understanding.
Behavioural therapies: exposure, systematic desensitisation, aversion therapy, token economies — built directly on conditioning.
Cognitive and cognitive-behavioural therapies (Beck, Ellis) target distorted thinking and behaviour together; CBT has the broadest evidence base across disorders.
Biomedical: SSRIs and other antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilisers such as lithium, ECT for severe depression, TMS, and psychosurgery as a rare last resort.
Third-wave approaches: mindfulness-based and acceptance-based therapies, dialectical behaviour therapy for borderline personality disorder.
Common factors: the therapeutic alliance predicts outcome across orientations; placebo effects are real and substantial.
Evidence-based practice integrates research evidence, clinical expertise and patient characteristics.
Deinstitutionalisation moved care to the community with mixed results; involuntary commitment raises legal and ethical questions about autonomy and risk.
Access is shaped by cost, insurance, workforce supply and stigma; cultural competence affects both engagement and outcome.

questions.prompt: A therapist gradually pairs relaxation with increasingly feared stimuli until the client can face the phobic object. This treatment is built directly on which learning principle?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation replaces the fear response with an incompatible relaxation response by pairing them — counterconditioning through classical conditioning.

questions.prompt: Two therapists using very different orientations achieve similar outcomes, and both report that the quality of the relationship matters most. Which finding does this reflect?
choices: Common factors such as the therapeutic alliance account for much of the shared benefit
questions.explanation: Common-factors research finds that alliance, empathy, expectations and structure contribute substantially across orientations, alongside technique-specific effects.

questions.prompt: Name the treatment approach with the broadest evidence base that combines changing distorted thinking with changing behaviour.
questions.explanation: Cognitive-behavioural therapy, from Beck's cognitive therapy and Ellis's rational emotive behaviour therapy, has the widest empirical support across anxiety, depression and many other conditions.
